title: The Compilation Pipeline
summary: Source text becomes running machine code through a fixed sequence of stages, each with its own artifact. Every other topic in this group is a deep dive into one stage of this map.

slides.markdown:
Compiling isn't one step — it's a pipeline of distinct stages, each consuming the previous stage's output and producing its own: source text becomes a token stream, becomes a syntax tree, becomes a checked tree, becomes an intermediate form, becomes optimized code, becomes machine instructions.

The reason to learn the pipeline before any single stage is that almost every compiler question an interviewer asks is really "which stage does this belong to": a syntax error is the parser's; an "undeclared variable" error is semantic analysis's; a missed optimization is the IR/optimizer's. Knowing the map tells you where to look.

This topic is the scaffold. Every later topic in this group — lexing, parsing, semantic analysis, IR, codegen, optimization — is a zoom-in on exactly one box in the diagram this topic draws.

![Full compilation pipeline from source text to machine code, split into front end and back end](assets/compilation-pipeline.svg)

Each box takes one specific input shape and produces one specific output shape — that's the whole design principle. `main() { return 1+2; }` becomes tokens (`main`, `(`, `)`, `{`, ...), then a tree, then a type-checked tree, then a flat IR instruction, then an optimized IR instruction, then a real `add` opcode.

slides.subTitle: One spectrum, not three separate things
slides.markdown:
All three run the same source language; they differ in **when** and **how far** they translate before execution actually happens.

A pure **compiler** (GCC, `rustc`) runs the whole pipeline ahead of time and produces machine code that a CPU runs directly — no translation step left at run time. A pure **interpreter** skips codegen entirely and executes the AST or an intermediate bytecode form directly, translating (or re-interpreting) as it goes, every single time. A **JIT** (V8, the JVM's HotSpot) starts by interpreting, then compiles the *hot* parts — the code paths actually running a lot — to machine code partway through execution, using runtime information an ahead-of-time compiler never has (which branch is actually taken, which types actually show up).

This is genuinely one spectrum of "how much of the pipeline runs before the program executes vs during," not three unrelated designs — the `runtimes` group covers the execution-time half of this spectrum in depth; this group covers the static half.

The pipeline splits cleanly into two halves with different jobs. The **front end** — lexer, parser, semantic analysis, IR generation — understands the *source language*: its syntax, its scoping rules, its type system. The **back end** — optimization, register allocation, instruction selection, codegen — understands the *target machine*: what instructions it has, how many registers, what a function call costs there.

The IR sitting between them is deliberately the seam: it's designed to not favor any one source language or any one target, so a front end never needs to know anything about x86 versus ARM, and a back end never needs to know anything about whether the source was Python-like or C-like.

slides.sectionTitle: Why the split pays for itself: LLVM
slides.markdown:
Splitting front end and back end at a shared IR means N languages and M targets need N front ends plus M back ends, not N×M compilers built from scratch. **LLVM** is the concrete, load-bearing example: Clang (C/C++), Rust's `rustc`, and Swift's compiler are three completely different front ends that all lower to **LLVM IR**, and from there share the exact same back end — the same optimization passes, the same register allocators, the same code generators for x86, ARM, RISC-V, and more.

Add a new source language and you write one front end and get every target LLVM already supports for free. Add a new CPU architecture and every existing front end gets to target it immediately. That leverage is the entire economic case for a pipelined, IR-centered compiler design rather than one monolithic per-language-per-target program.

Tracing `x = 1 + 2 * 3` through the pipeline:

```text
Source:   x = 1 + 2 * 3

Tokens:   IDENT(x) EQ NUM(1) PLUS NUM(2) STAR NUM(3)

AST:      Assign(x, Add(1, Mul(2, 3)))          # precedence already resolved

IR:       t1 = 2 * 3
          t2 = 1 + t1
          x  = t2

Asm:      MOV  R1, 2
          MUL  R1, R1, 3
          ADD  R1, R1, 1
          MOV  [x], R1
```

Notice what each stage adds: tokenizing just chops characters into units; parsing imposes structure (multiplication binds tighter, so it's nested inside the addition); IR generation flattens that tree into a linear sequence of simple operations; codegen picks concrete instructions and real registers.

slides.sectionTitle: Where different bugs are actually caught
slides.markdown:
| Stage | Example failure | What it looks like to you |
|---|---|---|
| Lexer | An invalid character (`@` where it's not allowed) | "Unexpected character" |
| Parser | Mismatched parentheses, missing semicolon | "Syntax error, expected X" |
| Semantic analysis | Undeclared variable, type mismatch | "Undefined symbol", "cannot assign string to int" |
| Optimization / codegen | (Rare, and usually a compiler bug) | Miscompiled or unexpectedly slow output |

A syntactically perfect program can still fail semantic analysis (`"a" + 3` in a statically typed language parses fine, and is still rejected). This table is a fast way to answer "where would this error actually come from" in an interview — match the *symptom's wording* to the stage whose job that check is.

The habit that costs candidates and working engineers alike: reasoning about "the compiler" as a black box instead of a sequence of stages, which makes it much harder to guess where a given bug or error actually originates.

"Why did `gcc` fail on this file" has a different debugging path depending on which stage failed — a parse error means the file's *structure* is wrong and no amount of fixing types will help; a linker error (a separate step entirely, after codegen, resolving symbols across compiled units) means the structure and types were fine but something the code references doesn't exist in any object file being linked. Conflating these wastes real debugging time chasing the wrong kind of fix.

The fix for this habit is exactly this topic: keep the stage boundaries in your head, and read an error message for which stage's vocabulary it's using before trying to fix it.

"Walk me through what happens when you run `gcc` on this file" is really asking whether you know the pipeline has real, separate stages with real intermediate artifacts, not whether you can recite compiler theory.

A solid answer names each stage and, ideally, that `gcc` itself is really a driver program invoking separate tools: **preprocessing** (macro expansion, `#include` resolution) produces expanded source; the **compiler proper** runs lex → parse → semantic analysis → IR → optimize → codegen, producing assembly; an **assembler** turns that assembly into an object file (machine code plus unresolved symbol references); and a **linker** combines object files and libraries, resolving every symbol reference into a final address, producing the executable. `gcc -c` stops after the object file; a plain `gcc` runs the linker too. Naming the assembler and linker as distinct steps — not just "compilation" — is what separates a strong answer from a shallow one.

slides.sectionTitle: One pipeline, many front ends and back ends
slides.markdown:
The pipeline shape in this topic isn't specific to C or to any one language — every mainstream ahead-of-time compiler follows it, with implementation details differing per stage. A dynamically typed language's "semantic analysis" stage does far less static checking than a statically typed one's (much of that work moves to runtime instead), but it's still a distinct stage doing scope resolution and some static checks.

What's genuinely universal: text goes in, structure comes out of parsing, meaning gets checked, an IR gets built and improved, and a target-specific back end turns that into something a CPU (or a VM, for interpreted/bytecode languages) can actually run. Every topic that follows zooms into exactly one of these boxes.
